Fetal & Maternal Monitoring During 
Labor and Birth 
NRBS 3410
Summer 2026

Intrapartum FHR monitoring is the single most 
common obstetric procedure in the US, 
impacting the lives of almost 8 million mothers 
and babies every year (ACOG 2008) 
The Joint Commission Identified “poor 
communication of abnormal FHR patterns” as a 
leading risk factor for preventable perinatal 
injury

Fetal Assessment During Labor
 Electronic fetal monitoring is a useful tool for visualizing 
fetal heart rate (FHR) patterns on monitor screen or 
printed tracing
 No evidence that EFM improves fetal outcomes in low 
risk pregnancies, increases risk for operative 
intervention and cesarean section
 Goal of monitoring is to identify changes in FHR 
indicating declining reserve or fetal compromise and 
guide interventions to promote fetal well being
 Intermittent auscultation, when used appropriately, can 
identify and predict fetal well being

Fetal Assessment Cont. 
 Fetal response to labor
 Labor is a period of physiologic stress for fetus
 Physiologic mechanisms of uterine contractions create a 
decrease in blood supply to the fetus for the duration of the 
contraction
 Frequent monitoring of fetal status is part of nursing care during 
labor
 Fetal oxygen supply must be maintained during labor to prevent 
fetal compromise

 Initial 10- to 20-minute continuous FHR assessment on 
entry into labor/birth area
 Completion of a prenatal and labor risk assessment on 
all clients
 Intermittent auscultation every 30 minutes during active 
labor for a low-risk woman and every 15 minutes for a 
high-risk woman
 During the second stage of labor, every 15 minutes for 
the low-risk woman and every 5 minutes for the high-
risk woman and during the pushing stage
Recommendation by AWHON, ACNM and ACOG for 
Fetal Monitoring

What We Monitor During Labor
 Maternal Hemodynamic Stability
 Uterine Contractions
 Frequency
 Duration
 Intensity
 Fetal Response to Contractions
 Fetal Heart Rate
 Changes over time
 Deceleration 
 Variability
 Accelerations

Uterine Contractions
 Uterine contractions are caused by release of the 
hormone oxytocin
 Uterine contractions need to occur with enough 
strength and have long enough duration to cause 
cervical dilation
 Placental blood flow is decreased for the duration of the 
uterine contraction
 Uterine contractions which last longer than expected 
(see phases of Stage I) or are stronger than necessary 
compromise the fetus through prolonged decreased 
blood flow.

Monitoring—cont’d 
 Fetal oxygen supply can be decreased because of reduction of blood 
flow through maternal vessels as result of:
 Maternal hypertension: chronic or pregnancy-induced 
hypertension
 Hypotension caused by supine maternal position, hemorrhage, 
epidural analgesia, or anesthesia
 Hypovolemia caused by hemorrhage
 Reduction of oxygen content in maternal blood as result of 
hemorrhage or severe anemia
 Alterations in fetal circulation with compression of umbilical 
cord during contraction 
 Reduction in blood flow to intervillous space 
in placenta

EFM
External Fetal Monitoring-records fetal and uterine activity tracing
  1)  Tocotransducer-pressure sensitive-placed on fundus
 Detects changes in uterine pressure
2) Ultrasound transducer-
 Fetal heart rate baseline
 Variability in fetal heart rate
 Accelerations
 Decelerations
INVASIVE: Internal Fetal Monitoring-scalp electrode- small spiral wire placed 
under fetal scalp records fetal heart tracing.  Intrauterine pressure catheter 
(IUPC) monitors intensity of contraction from inside
 More accurate, no loss of contact with fetal movement
 No maternal artifact
 Membranes must be ruptured to place 
 IUPC can measure true strength of contraction

External Electronic Fetal Monitoring (EFM) uses doppler and 
tocometer transducers

Location of the fetal heart rate (FHR) in relation to the more 
commonly seen fetal positions. The FHR is heard more clearly over 
the fetal back.

Criteria for Using 
Fetal Scalp Electrode
 Ruptured membranes
 Cervical dilation of at least 2 cm
 Present fetal part low enough to allow 
placement of the scalp electrode

Electronic Fetal Monitoring…3 questions to ask
Terminology – What do I call it?
Interpretation – What does it mean?
Management – What do I do about it?

Key Terms Related to Fetal Heart Rate 
 Accelerations-increase in fetal hear rate (FHR) by 15 
beats per minute (BPM) lasting 15 seconds but less than 
30 seconds. Response to contractions or stimuli
 Artifacts-changes in FHR tracings attributed to maternal 
heart rate or change in doppler placement
 Baseline fetal heart rate-110-160 BPM “normal”
 Determined over 10 minute tracing segment that 
excludes periods of tachycardia or bradycardia 
 Fetal tachycardia=baseline greater than 160 lasting 
longer than 10 minutes
 Fetal bradycardia=baseline less than 110 lasting longer 
than 10 minutes
 Ominous when accompanied by loss of variability and late 
decelerations

Fetal Heart Rate  
 Baseline FHR 110-160 BPM
 Baseline rate is average during 10-minute segment, 
excluding: 
 Accelerations-increase of 15 BPM  lasting 15 BPM 
 Decelerations-decrease of 15 BPM lasting 15 BPM
 Periods of marked variability
 Normal range at term 110 to 160 beats/min

Mean FHR rounded to increments of 5 bpm in a 10-minute 
window, excluding accelerations, decelerations and periods of 
marked variability

Accelerations
 Accelerations
 Increase in fetal hear rate (FHR) by 15 beats 
per minute (BPM) 
 Lasting at least 15 seconds but less than 30 
seconds
 In response to contractions or stimuli
Fig. 17-6. Accelerations of fetal heart rate.

Electronic Fetal Monitoring Decelerations
 Deceleration-transient decrease in FHR
 Early deceleration-gradual decrease with nadir (lowest point) 
mirroring apex of contraction
 Common in active labor and 2nd stage
 Common with vacuum extraction 
 Related to fetal head compression 
NOT indication of fetal distress
 Late deceleration-symmetrical decrease in FHR
 Nadir occurs after the contraction (doesn’t mirror)
 Delay is related to uteroplacental insufficiency
 Maternal labor hypotension, gestational hypertension, 
placental aging-post term, hyperstimulation from 
oxytocin
 Variable deceleration-sudden decrease in FHR with sharp 
decline and sharp return. 
 Often related to compression of the umbilical cord.
Fig. 17-7. Deceleration patterns. A, Early.
Fig. 17-7. Deceleration patterns. B, Late.
Fig. 17-7. Deceleration patterns. D, Variable.

Fetal Heart Rate Patterns—cont’d 
 Changes in FHR
 Prolonged decelerations: FHR 15 beats/min below and 
lasting more than 2 minutes
Fig. 17-7. Deceleration patterns. C, Prolonged.

Nursing Care Management 
 EFM pattern recognition
 Must evaluate five components of an FHR tracing
 Baseline-within normal range
 Variability- moderate, minimal, absent or marked
 Accelerations – present or not
 Early decelerations- early decelerations present or not
 Late or variable decelerations- present or not
 Determine whether intervention is needed
 Maternal repositioning may resolve most FHR issues
 Identify indications to expedite birth
 Prolonged late or variable decelerations
 Fetal bradycardia
 Fetal tachycardia

EFM Variability 
 Baseline variability-fluctuations in baseline-
parasympathetic and sympathetic systems
 Moment to moment or beat to beat HR changes
 Moderate-normal 6-25 BPM fluctuation
 Minimal- < 5 BPM- 
 Absent- no visible variability
 Marked- > 25 BPM
Fig. 17-5. Fetal heart rate variability. C, Moderate.
Fig. 17-5. Fetal heart rate variability. A, Absent or undetected.
Fig. 17-5. Fetal heart rate variability. B, Minimal.
Fig. 17-5. Fetal heart rate variability. D, Marked.

Variability Problems
 Absent/minimal indication of fetal acidemia 2° to
 uteroplacental insufficiency
 cord compression
 maternal hypotension
 uterine hyperstimulation (too frequent/too long ctx)
Nursing Interventions to treat absent variability
 Aimed at improving uteroplacental perfusion
 Maternal lateral positioning 
 Increase IV fluids
 Administer Oxygen @ 8-10L via face mask
FHR Decelerations

Nurse’s Role
 Identification of FHR patterns
 Category I- 
 Category II-
 Category III
 Interventions-
 Maternal positioning
 Documentation
 Timely communication
 Follow up

Category I Tracing
 Category 1 Tracing: Normal 
Predictive of normal fetal acid-base status
 Baseline HR 110-160 bpm
 Baseline variability: moderate
 Accelerations: may be present or absent (fetal 
movement related)
 Decelerations: Early may be present 
 NO LATE OR VARIABLE DECELERATIONS

Category III Tracing
 Category III Tracing: 
  Predictive of ABNORMAL FETAL ACID/BASE STATUS
 Fetal Bradycardia (<110 bpm) 
 Recurrent late decelerations
 Recurrent variable decelerations
 Sinusoidal FHR pattern

Category II Tracing = Everything Else
 Category II Tracing: Indeterminant: 
 Not predictive of abnormal fetal acid-balance status
 Fetal tachycardia present (>160 bpm)
 Fetal Bradycardia (<110 bpm) NOT accompanied by ABSENT baseline variability
 Absent baseline variability NOT accompanied by recurrent decelerations
 Minimal or Marked variability
 Recurrent late decelerations with moderate baseline variability
 Recurrent variable decelerations accompanied by minimal or moderate variability 
overshoots (shoulders)
 Prolonged decelerations > 2minutes but < 10 minutes

Remember: Interventions 
• Intervention should address the probable cause
• Placental insufficiency vs. Cord compression
• Hypertonic contractions
• Maternal hypotension 
 Most decelerations can be alleviated by changes in the 
mother’s position
 Additional interventions:
 Stop pitocin stimulation
 Increased IV fluid rate
 Administration of supplemental oxygen
 Modified pushing
 Amnioinfusion

Key Points
 Fetal well-being during labor is gauged by response of FHR to 
UCs
 FHR characteristics include baseline FHR and periodic changes 
in FHR
 Monitoring of fetal well-being includes:
 FHR assessment
 Watching for meconium-stained amniotic fluid
 Assessment of maternal vital signs and uterine activity
 Responsibility of nurse to: 
 Assess FHR patterns
 Implement independent nursing interventions
 Report Category II or III patterns to physician or nurse-
midwife
